title: Tuppence and the Whispering Peaks
markdown:
Tuppence was not the sort of ogre who collected wart-covered noses or unsuspecting travellers. He was a solid fellow, shoulders like a boulder that had survived too many winters, hands the size of dinner plates when they were not busy with a patch of particularly stubborn cabbages. The cabbages grew behind a cottage that smelled of damp earth and boiled roots, and Tuppence talked to them as if they might answer, which they never did, being cabbages. His kindness ran quiet, like bees in a meadow, which did not stop most people from tiptoeing around the width of him.

His companion was Skipper, a cat of sleek shadow and emerald chips for eyes. Skipper held opinions on most matters and delivered them from sun-drenched windowsills, usually by yawning.

The trouble began, as it often does, with a lost pet. Not a dragon’s roar. Not a wizard’s cackle. Gribble, Tuppence’s fluffy purple griffin, had a talent for napping in inconvenient places, like a cloud that had lost its timetable. This time he had vanished into the jagged, cloud-kissed spires of the Whispering Peaks. Tuppence regarded those heights with an unspoken wobble in the knees. Sheer drops. Wind that sounded as if it had been sighing since last century. He looked up, and his stomach tightened without asking permission.

“The Peaks,” he rumbled to Skipper, distant thunder after rain. “They do look rather high, don’t they?”

Skipper, draped over a sun-warmed stone as if he owned the mountain range, opened a tiny pink cavern of a yawn and closed it again.

Tuppence trudged toward the mountains, great boots crunching frosty heather. He met the wizard Peregrin on the way. Peregrin was a man of many robes and even more pronouncements. His beard, a magnificent cascade of grey, trailed tiny sparks when he was excited or indignant, which was most of the time. He was currently having a loud disagreement with a cluster of villagers whose faces had gone the colour of worry.

“The berries!” Peregrin declared, theatrical as a man addressing an invisible opera house. “They taste precisely like yesterday’s forgotten socks left to ferment in a damp cupboard! A minor inconvenience, perhaps, for those with less refined palates.”

The villagers grumbled. A minor inconvenience? Their harvest. Their livelihood. The season growing short.

“Ah, Tuppence!” Peregrin flourished a hand. “Just the brute for brute work, as they say. Though this situation requires a touch more finesse. I am attempting to banish this ghastly sock-flavour with a Grand Frost-Warding Spell. A touch theatrical, perhaps, but supremely effective. Though,” he added, peering, “I detect a hint of something else. A scent of lost griffin, perhaps?”

Tuppence blinked. He had no idea how a wizard smelled a griffin. He just wanted Gribble.

A shadow fell, larger than any cloud. With a rustle of scales like diamond wind-chimes, a dragon landed with surprising grace. Ignis was no furnace with wings. Rainbow scales. Ember eyes. Manners that could have been bottled.

“Good day to you all,” Ignis purred, warm honey over smooth stones. “I overheard talk of a culinary calamity. Dragons have a discerning palate. My mother taught me a rather effective method for desocketifying fruits.”

Peregrin puffed. “Thank you, noble Ignis. A generous offer. But I have matters well in hand. Refined arcane energies, not draconic zest, however well-intentioned.” A faint sizzle from his fingertips toward the wilting bushes.

Ignis tilted a magnificent head. “If you are quite sure. Though sometimes a little blast of concentrated warmth, properly aimed, might just… ah.” He let out a gentle puff of smoke that smelled of cinnamon and old parchment. The bushes shivered as if a cold breath had passed over them.

“By the Great Grimoire!” Peregrin sputtered, beard crackling. “You’ve made them taste like old gravy now. A decidedly worse fate than socks.”

Tuppence watched the rivalry simmer, flamboyant wizard and polite dragon, each eager to outdo the other with assistance nobody had asked to be quite so assisted. His knees remembered waterfalls. Gribble was up there, probably dreaming of cloud-fluff.

The Whispering Peaks were not for people who preferred solid ground. Jagged edges clawed at the sky. The wind howled through crevices as if it had been practising for a very long funeral. Tuppence pressed on anyway, Skipper trotting at his heels and pausing now and then to groom with the air of a creature whose own fur was the most vital task in the range.

They reached a chasm, a dark mouth that swallowed light. The bridge across it was ancient stone, remarkably narrow and decidedly crooked, like a forgotten smile on a grumpy face. It trembled with every gust and groaned like an old man asked to do yard work.

“This,” Tuppence murmured, tighter than usual, “is most inconvenient. Most inconvenient indeed.”

Skipper’s fur bristled. A tiny black statue of apprehension.

Tuppence was steeling himself to set one broad boot on the groaning stone when he heard a faint distressed chirp. Higher up, clinging to a windswept ledge like a forgotten shelf, was Gribble. Purple plumage snagged in thorny vines, thorns like tiny teeth.

Down below, Ignis had decided to help Peregrin further. The wizard was coaxing a shy sunbeam to warm the berries. Ignis, believing the problem was a lack of sparkle, breathed shimmering golden dust over the bushes. The berries glowed an alarming green and emitted a faint persistent zzzzzzt, like a beetle trapped in a jar.

“They now taste of static electricity,” Peregrin wailed. “This is an outrage. I am calm.” His voice suggested a man trying to balance six fragile teacups on his head.

Tuppence, gaze fixed on Gribble, saw more than a lost pet. He saw a griffin who liked high perches, who felt safer off the ground. He saw the vines humming. Gribble’s feathers were sensitive. The musical vibration had drawn him up, and the thorns had kept him.

This was not a moment for grand magic or booming pronouncements. It was a moment for quiet, sturdy sense. Tuppence stepped onto the trembling crooked bridge. Stone groaned. Wind bit. Below, golden dust settled like strange luminous snow, and the berry bushes hummed an electric song. He thought of his cabbage patch, as safe as a settled burrow, and put the thought away. Gribble needed him. Discomfort, not sacrifice. A willing walk.

His feet were large and, usefully, broad. He moved with a deliberateness that made the precariousness look faintly embarrassed. One boot. Pause. The other. The bridge complained in a language of grit and old mortar. Skipper did not follow. Tuppence did not blame him. The world shrank to weathered stone and worried chirps. Wind found the gaps in his collar. Below, the berry bushes kept their electric song, as if the valley were humming through its teeth. He reached the ledge. With immense patient care, large gentle fingers, he began to untangle Gribble. The vines, still vibrating, pricked his hide. Purple down came away on the thorns. He paid them no mind, except to be slower.

“Who could have guessed,” Skipper muttered from the safer side, “that a dragon’s well-meaning dust would be the final buzzing straw?”

As Tuppence freed Gribble, a final surge of golden dust from Ignis, who was adding a touch more sparkle for good measure, landed on the vines. The humming intensified, then ceased with a soft satisfying pop. The vines went inert and let go. Gribble, free and a little flustered, nestled into Tuppence’s broad shoulder, purring like a kitten who had discovered cream.

With the dust settled and the vines quiet, the over-excited magic in the berries faded. The static fizz vanished. The zzzzzzt died. Villagers peeked from their homes, then ventured out. They picked one berry. Then another.

“They taste like berries again,” one said, astonished. “Remarkably normal berries. Not a hint of sock, gravy, or even static.”

Peregrin stared, mouth agape, beard momentarily sparkless. Ignis preened.

“Ah, yes,” he said sagely. “Sometimes a little disruption is all that is needed to restore natural order.”

Tuppence, holding Gribble, simply nodded. He had not cast a spell, uttered a boast, or raised his voice. He had been Tuppence, large hands, even larger patience. Wizard and dragon exchanged a look that might, on a generous day, have been called respect. Peregrin’s beard remembered how to spark, then thought better of it. Ignis tasted a berry with the gravity of a sommelier and admitted, as if it hurt, that ordinary was an achievement.

The valley had its berries. The griffin was safe, a warm purple weight against Tuppence’s neck, still smelling faintly of thorn and static. They came down the long way, because Tuppence had had enough of bridges for one afternoon. Later that week, when a flock of adventurous birds nested close to a high cliff, Tuppence watched them without a tremor in the knees. The Peaks still loomed. They no longer felt like a dare. Skipper was already dreaming of a sunny spot and a well-deserved, sock-free berry tart. The cabbages, when Tuppence got home, were as stubborn as ever. He found that reassuring. Gribble took the windowsill. Skipper took the cushion. Nobody mentioned socks.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
